newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austria says police on tail of 10 bomb suspects.
newsitem.headline: Austria says police on tail of 10 bomb suspects.

text.p: Austria's security chief said on Monday police were tailing 10 suspects following a threat last week to bomb prominent people in Austria and abroad.

The warning, which came in the middle of campaigning for European parliamentary and Vienna state elections next Sunday, said eight people were targetted in a fresh bombing offensive by a suspected rightwing extremist group.
"For the past few days we have been shadowing 10 suspects around the clock," the head of Austria's security department Michael Sika told Austrian television.
He gave no further details of the surveillance, which was an indication of some progress in the hunt for the perpetrators of a three-year letter bomb campaign.
Chancellor Franz Vranitzky's name appeared on the list of targets sent to a current affairs magazine last Tuesday by the group which calls itself the Bajuwarian Liberation Army (BLA).
Bodyguards, who usually melt into the background on public occasions, now remain close to the chancellor, particularly during outdoor election campaigning.
The BLA have claimed responsibility for around 20 letter bombs since December 1993 which have injured some 11 people, nearly all immigrants or figures linked to foreigner issues.
A bomb that killed four gypsy men last year may be connected to the same group, security sources said.

Chief inspector Robert Sturm, head of the Interior Ministry anti-terrorist unit, said police had been alerted to around 80 suspect packages since the threat was issued but all turned out to be harmless.
"It's all calm at the moment but things are likely to remain touchy until the elections," he added.
Sika said the number eight was of particular significance to the extremists and called on Austrians to be especially cautious on Tuesday, October 8.
The documentation sent by the BLA stated that the latest threat was connected with jail terms handed out to two confessed neo-Nazis, Peter Binder and Franz Radl.
The two men were the only suspects held for the first wave of letter bombs. They were acquitted last December of those charges but jailed for eight years for neo-Nazi activities.
The group said it planned to blow up eight public figures, but only Vranitzky's name has been released.

Most explosions claimed by the BLA have been rigged to letters or packages but security officials have taken the latest threat more seriously as bombs, and not letter bombs, were referred to for the first time.
"It's not so much letter bombs that we fear, but bomb explosions," Sika said.

Little is known about the BLA. Police believe it could be a neo-Nazi organisation but other officials say the group may be made up of a handful of middle-aged men obsessed with reuniting German-speaking peoples in Bavaria, the Alps and the Danube River -- a distinct region which existed between the sixth and 12th centuries.
